title: A settled leaning toward

words.nuance: The indulgent one: **penchant** attaches to a pleasure you enjoy having, usually a small or slightly frivolous one (loud ties, gossip, good champagne). It's what friends would list about you with a smile, never what a report would record about you.

The *pre*- is load-bearing: a **predilection** is already formed before the case arrives, so it colours judgement rather than just describing taste — a judge's predilection for lenient sentences. It's the most formal of the set and the most useful for quiet editorialising (*a predilection for lost causes*), and it stays mild: never a passion, only a standing preference.

The vice word. A **proclivity** is toward *doing* something disreputable — gambling, brawling, lying — and it implies the leaning is settled and characteristic, part of who you are. Attach it to something harmless and it turns arch or sounds like an accusation.

The clinical, measurable one: a **propensity** is a trait you've been assessed as having, which is why lawyers, psychologists and statisticians own the word. Unlike the others, it applies to things as readily as people — steel has a propensity to fracture in cold — and it names a rate of acting, not a taste.

The only member that needn't involve behaviour at all. An **affinity** claims a built-in match: an affinity *for* something is attraction (elements for oxygen, a person for jazz), an affinity *with* or *between* things is plain resemblance (Sanskrit and Latin) with no feeling involved. Nothing here is a fault, and nothing here is indulgence.

The only adjective, and the only one that isn't a standing trait: to be **inclined** is to lean on *this* question, right now (*inclined to agree*), which is why it's committee-speak — the exit door stays open. Everything else in this group is something you carry around; this is a position you're halfway to taking.

core: All of these name a leaning that is already there before any particular choice comes up — a settled tilt rather than a decision made on the spot. They differ on three axes: how respectable the thing leaned toward is, who is doing the describing (a friend, a novelist, a prosecutor, a statistician), and whether the leaning is a lasting trait or just today's lean. Miss those axes and they look interchangeable; catch them and each one is nearly forced by its context.
exam_note: The trap is valence: the sentence supplies a harmless pleasure and offers proclivity/propensity, or supplies a vice and offers penchant — read the object of the leaning, not the leaning itself.
